Part1.title: Game Client Development
content: I specialize in <1><2>game client development</2></1> with hands-on experience from my internship at <1><2>Tencent Lightspeed Studio</2></1>.

I am skilled in using <1><2>RenderDoc</2></1> for frame capturing and reverse-engineering complex rendering workflows. During my internship, I conducted in-depth analysis of the rendering techniques used in several recent games, including <1><2>Call of Duty: Black Ops VI</2></1> and <1><2>Infinity Nikki</2></1>.
With a strong foundation in <1><2>OpenGL</2></1> and a portfolio of related projects, I also have a working knowledge of <1><2>Vulkan</2></1>.
Additionally, I am familiar with <1><2>Unreal Engine</2></1> and have experience developing custom plugins to extend its functionality.

Part2.title: Programming Languages
content: I am highly familiar with <1><2>C++</2></1>, having completed <1><2>Advanced C++20 Programming</2></1> and developed numerous related projects such as a mini-engine.
I specialize in profiling programs and resolving performance bottlenecks efficiently, while maintaining strict and consistent coding standards.
In addition, I have extensive experience with <1><2>Python</2></1>, which has been an essential tool throughout my graduate research.
Beyond typical scripting, I have developed various plugins using Python, including those for <1><2>ZBrush</2></1>, <1><2>3ds Max</2></1>, <1><2>Blender</2></1>, and <1><2>RenderDoc</2></1>.

Part3.title: Research
content: My research focuses on real-time relighting algorithms based on <1><2>2D Gaussian Splatting</2></1>.
I have a solid background in <1><2>deep learning</2></1> and am familiar with <1><2>Python</2></1> and <1><2>PyTorch</2></1>.
I am skilled at implementing academic papers and rapidly understanding their key contributions.

Abstract.title: Abstract
content1: Pika Engine is a self-developed mini-engine designed to apply and realize the knowledge I’ve acquired through hands-on implementation. Development has been on hold since I started my internship at <1>Tencent Lightspeed Studios</1>, but I plan to revisit and upgrade the engine when time permits in the future.

The current Pika Engine supports both 2D and 3D scenes. In 2D scenes, it uses Quads as primitives and supports <1>Batch Rendering</1> to render the entire scene with a minimal number of draw calls. It also supports <1>2D physics simulation</1>.
content2: For 3D scenes, it currently supports <1>Skybox</1>, <1>Lighting</1>, and <1>Shadows</1>, and allows importing Mesh data in formats such as OBJ and FBX. The current material system is relatively simple and uses predefined <1>Blinn-Phong</1> materials. Support for <1>physically based rendering (PBR)</1> materials will be added in future versions.

ECS.title: Entity Component System
content1: The <1>Entity Component System (ECS)</1> is a powerful architectural pattern widely adopted in modern game engines, including <1>Unreal Engine (UE)</1> and <1>Unity</1>, due to its flexibility, scalability, and performance benefits.

Pika Engine utilizes the third-party library <3>entt</3> to implement its own ECS (Entity Component System). The separation of data and logic allows Pika to efficiently manage entities and their associated components, such as <1>UUID</1>, <1>Material</1>, <1>Mesh</1>, and others.
content2: As shown in the figure above, you can easily configure component properties, add or remove components, and perform other operations through the UI.

Lighting&Shadow.title: Lighting & Shadow
content1: The Pika engine currently supports point lights, spotlights, and directional lights, each with integrated shadow mapping. Additional lighting types, such as area lights and emissive surfaces, are planned for future updates.

To reduce common shadow mapping artifacts—particularly <1>moiré patterns</1> and <1>surface acne</1>—the engine leverages <1>reverse-Z</1> buffering alongside enhanced depth precision techniques to improve visual fidelity. <1>Depth bias</1> remains a particularly tricky aspect; a dynamic, slope-aware biasing strategy is planned for future implementation to adapt to varying light directions and surface normals, which is expected to effectively mitigate such artifacts.
content2: More advanced shadowing techniques such as <1>Cascaded Shadow Maps (CSM)</1>, <1>Percentage Closer Filtering (PCF)</1>, and <1>Percentage Closer Soft Shadows (PCSS)</1> have not yet been implemented, but are planned for future integration as the engine evolves.

Material.title: Material
content: In terms of material support, the Pika engine currently offers a configurable <1>Blinn-Phong</1> shading model. Future updates will introduce support for physically based rendering (PBR) materials, as well as comprehensive import and export functionality for mainstream 3D model formats along with their associated material data. Widely used embedded-material formats such as <1>FBX</1>, <1>glb</1>, and <1>glTF</1> will be supported to ensure seamless integration with popular modeling tools and asset pipelines.

Render.title: Render
content: Pika's rendering interface is designed using the Factory design pattern, with a clear separation between the rendering abstraction layer and the underlying graphics API. The original intent behind this design was to ensure flexibility and allow support for multiple graphics backends such as <1>OpenGL</1>, <1>DirectX 12</1>, <1>Vulkan</1>, and <1>Metal</1>.

However, I later realized a key limitation with this approach: designing the API to be compatible with all backends means I have to accommodate the least capable one—namely OpenGL. Since OpenGL lacks support for modern features like command buffers and multithreaded rendering, this severely restricts the potential of my rendering system.

As a result, I plan to fully drop OpenGL in the future and adopt a Vulkan-only backend. Vulkan is not only cross-platform—helping reduce development overhead—but also aligns better with my expertise, allowing me to implement more advanced and efficient rendering features.

Physics.title: Physics
content: Physics systems are now an essential part of modern game engines. Currently, the Pika engine only supports physics simulation in 2D scenes. I integrated the open-source <3>Box2D</3> library to add physical collision detection and 2D rigid body components for entities in 2D scenes. For 3D scenes, NVIDIA <4>PhysX</4> is intended to be used for implementing physical simulations, with more advanced physics features planned for future development.

Serialization.title: Serialization
content1: Serialization in Pika includes both scene serialization and deserialization. When saving the current scene state, Pika serializes key scene information into a <3>YAML</3>-based .pika file. You can import a scene by simply dragging it from the <1>Content Browser</1> into the <1>Viewport</1>, or by using the Import option from the menu bar.
content2: In addition, model files are also part of the serialization system. Currently, model data import and export are supported through the <3>Assimp</3> library. To load a 3D model, you can simply drag the corresponding file into the Model Component section.

Conclusion.title: Conclusion
content: The Pika engine is a work-in-progress project. During my internship, I had limited time to keep it updated. I originally started this engine to integrate the graphics algorithms I had learned into a single impressive project and to use it as a showcase during interviews. Building the core framework consumed a significant amount of my energy, leaving little time to implement various rendering algorithms and engine features.

Today, I have gained much deeper knowledge in computer graphics. I’ve analyzed the rendering techniques of cutting-edge games like <1><2><3>Call of Duty: Black Ops 6</3></2></1> and <1><2><4>Infinity Nikki</4></2></1>, and I’m currently studying the rendering concepts presented in <1><2>Real-Time Rendering, 4th Edition</2></1>. I now better understand the complexity behind top-tier engines like Unreal Engine, particularly systems such as <1>Lumen</1> and <1>Nanite</1>.

With this experience, I’m more prepared than ever to advance the development of the Pika engine. In the future, Pika will focus heavily on 3D capabilities, introducing scripting support, a material system, and more rendering features including—but not limited to—anti-aliasing, ambient occlusion, and global illumination. I also plan to fully abandon OpenGL in favor of Vulkan to achieve more efficient rendering. Stay tuned.

CODAnalysisPage.Title: Call of Duty: Black Ops VI Analysis

Abstract.title: Abstract
content: <1>Disclaimer</1>: This content is intended solely for educational and project showcase purposes. If any infringement is found, please <3>contact me</3> for prompt removal.

This blog presents a summary of my <1>rendering analysis</1> of <1><2><4>Call of Duty: Black Ops VI</4></2></1> and a review of the associated rendering techniques. To keep the blog concise, only key highlights are covered here — for the full analysis, please download the detailed documentation. The full analysis document is available for download via the <1><5>Doc</5></1> button below the title.

DOF.title: Depth of Field
content: Depth of Field

AA.title: Anti-Aliasing
AA.content0: <1>The anti-aliasing techniques used in the game</1>:
content1: The anti-aliasing primarily combines spatial-domain <1><2><3>SMAA</3></2></1> (Subpixel Morphological Anti-Aliasing) with temporal <1><2><4>TAA</4></2></1> (Temporal Anti-Aliasing), and builds upon this with <1><2><5>NIS</5></2></1> (NVIDIA Image Scaling) upscaling to enhance resolution while adaptively sharpening edges, resulting in high-quality anti-aliasing. The image below illustrates the dispatches corresponding to each algorithm within a captured frame.

SMAA.title: SMAA
content1: <1><2><3>SMAA (Subpixel Morphological Anti-Aliasing)</3></2></1> is a widely used post-processing anti-aliasing algorithm, particularly effective in PC games with deferred rendering pipelines. It is an improvement over <1><2><4>MLAA (Morphological Anti-Aliasing)</4></2></1>, offering more accurate edge detection and subpixel precision to enhance sharpness and anti-aliasing quality.
<1>SMAA is mainly divided into three stages, as shown below:</1>
SMAA.content2: SMAA (Subpixel Morphological Anti-Aliasing) improves upon MLAA by introducing a more accurate <1>edge detection</1> method. Instead of relying solely on color discontinuities, SMAA incorporates <1>local contrast adaptation</1> to better distinguish true geometric edges from texture noise or fine details. This significantly reduces false positives and preserves image sharpness. By detecting diagonal and subpixel edges, SMAA achieves high-quality anti-aliasing with minimal performance overhead, making it ideal for deferred rendering pipelines. The following shows the edge detection results of SMAA in the game, where the red channel represents vertical edges and the green channel represents horizontal edges.
SMAA.content3: As shown in the figure below, the texture on the left is the SMAA weight lookup table (LUT), which stores blending weights for edge patterns such as L-shapes, T-junctions, and crosses. The texture on the right shows the final blending weights computed using the LUT.
SMAA.content4: The third stage is performed in a subsequent dispatch together with <1>TAA</1> (which will be discussed in the next section), where SMAA utilizes the computed blending weights to <1>blend neighboring pixels</1>, resulting in a high-quality anti-aliasing effect.

TAA.title: TAA
TAA.content1: <1><2><3>TAA (Temporal Anti-Aliasing)</3></2></1> is a commonly used anti-aliasing technique in modern games. It blends pixel information from the current frame with data from previous frames using motion vectors, effectively reducing jagged edges and temporal flickering. Compared to spatial techniques like <1>SMAA</1> or <1>FXAA</1>, TAA handles sub-pixel details better but may introduce artifacts like ghosting if not properly filtered.
TAA.content2: As shown in the figure above, the game implements TAA by using <1>motion vectors</1>, <1>translucency masks</1>, and <1>SMAA weights</1> from the current frame and two previous frames to perform temporal anti-aliasing and reduce flickering artifacts. The final result of combining SMAA and TAA is shown at the bottom.

NIS.title: NIS
NIS.content1: <1><2><3>NVIDIA Image Scaling (NIS)</3></2></1> is a spatial <1>upscaling</1> and <1>sharpening</1> technique developed by NVIDIA. It aims to boost image resolution and visual clarity with minimal performance overhead. Unlike <1><2><4>DLSS</4></2></1>, NIS does not rely on deep learning, making it compatible with a wider range of GPUs and platforms. While NIS is not strictly an anti-aliasing method, its adaptive sharpening significantly enhances edge quality and closely relates to anti-aliasing in this context, hence it is analyzed here as part of the anti-aliasing pipeline.
NIS.content2: The image above shows the result after NIS upscaling (from 912×512 to 1366×768). The inputs here are the <1>NIS scaling factor table</1> and the <1>NIS sharpening factor table</1>.

AO.title: Ambient Occlusion
AO.content0: <1>The ambient occlusion techniques used in the game</1>:
content1: <2>Call of Duty: Black Ops 6</2> uses <1><2><3>GTAO</3></2></1> to compute high-quality ambient occlusion. As shown in the image above, the AO quality is visibly excellent. In this implementation, GTAO-related data is calculated in a single dispatch using inputs such as <1>normal</1> and <1>depth</1>, and is later combined with shadow computations to generate a shared <1>visibility texture</1> (which will be covered in the upcoming <4>Shadow section</4>), which is then used in the final rendering process.

GTAO.title: GTAO
GTAO.content1: GTAO works by subdividing the view-direction hemisphere at each pixel into a set of angular “<1>slices</1>,” then for each slice sampling the maximum visible angle—that is, the largest depth interval along that direction that remains unoccluded. These per-slice visibility values are weighted by both distance falloff and the surface normal’s orientation, accumulated across all slices, and normalized to yield a single ambient occlusion coefficient. By focusing on the maximum unblocked angle per slice rather than dense random samples, GTAO achieves high-quality AO with fewer probes, lower noise, and efficient performance.
GTAO.content2: In Call of Duty: Black Ops 6, GTAO is computed in a single dispatch. The image below shows some of its <1>inputs</1>: the depth buffer (including both a <1>standard Z-buffer</1> and a <1>reversed Z-buffer</1>), the <1>normal buffer</1> and a <1>random texture</1> for constructing the hemisphere’s base sampling directions and introducing per-slice randomness to suppress noise. There are actually additional inputs—such as data from the previous frame—but limited shader readability prevented a full reverse-engineering of every detail. Overall, the algorithm follows the standard GTAO approach—performing hemisphere sampling and per-slice integration to compute the final AO value.
GTAO.content3: Shown below are the outputs, both in <1>R32_UINT</1> format: the image on the left displays the computed <1>AO values</1>, and the one on the right shows the <1><3>Bent Normal</3></1> (the weighted average direction of all unoccluded sample rays over the hemisphere around the surface normal, used to guide environment and indirect lighting sampling).

Reflection.title: Reflection
Reflection.content0: <1>The reflection rendering techniques used in the game</1>:
Reflection.content1: In the game, reflections are implemented by combining <1>SSR</1> with <1>reflection probes</1>. Since SSR cannot capture objects outside the screen, reflection probes are often used as a fallback at the edges of the screen to provide smooth transitions and prevent visual artifacts caused by SSR’s inherent limitations.

SSR.title: SSR
SSR.content1: <1><2><3>Screen-Space Reflections (SSR)</3></2></1> leverage the <1>depth</1> and <1>normal</1> buffers of the already rendered frame to perform stepwise sampling (ray marching) along the reflection vector in screen space. By comparing depths, the algorithm determines when the ray “hits” visible geometry, then samples the reflection color from the color buffer. The entire process can be simply understood as performing ray marching on a 2D image, as illustrated below.
SSR.content2: It should be noted that Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 uses SSR optimized with a <1>Hierarchical Z-Buffer (HZB)</1> to accelerate ray-marching intersection. Since per-pixel ray marching in screen space is prohibitively expensive, a Hierarchical Z-Buffer is pre-generated to speed up this process. The image below illustrates how the HZB optimizes the intersection steps.
SSR.content3: The image below shows the dispatch used to pre-generate the Hierarchical Z-Buffer (HZB) for the game's subsequent SSR ray-marching. It also employs a <1>ping-pong</1> buffering strategy that alternates reads and writes between two identical HZB slices, eliminating read/write conflicts within a single pass, enabling efficient multi-level downsampling without rebinding or reallocating textures at each mip level.

ReflectionProbe.title: Reflection Probe
ReflectionProbe.content1: <1><2><3>Reflection probes</3></2></1> generate prefiltered cube maps at specific positions in the scene and sample from different mip levels based on material roughness to provide high-frequency environment reflections for areas outside SSR coverage or occluded regions. Blending multiple probes achieves smooth transitions while balancing performance and visual quality. Below is a demonstration of a Reflection Probe in <1>Unity</1>.
ReflectionProbe.content2: Here I found direct evidence of reflection probe usage in the shader. I won’t elaborate further here.

GI.title: Global Illumination
GI.content0: <1>The global illumination techniques used in the game</1>:

Shadow.title: Shadow
Shadow.content0: <1>The shadow techniques used in the game</1>:
Shadow.content1: After reverse-engineering the shader, I was surprised to find that Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 doesn’t use more advanced, high-quality shadow techniques (like <3>SDF shadows</3>, <4>contact shadows</4>, <5>micro shadows</5>, etc.). It’s really just <6>CSM</6> combined with <7>PCF</7> edge anti-aliasing using Vogel Disk Rotation sampling—presumably because a fast-paced first-person shooter demands high FPS, and shadow quality isn’t the top priority.

CSM.title: CSM
CSM.content1: You can see in the image below the three 2K-resolution CSM shadow maps, which correspond to the near, middle, and far slices of the view frustum.

PCF.title: PCF
PCF.content1: Based on my shader reverse‐engineering, the shadow‐edge anti‐aliasing appears to be implemented with a 16‐sample PCF using <3>Vogel‐disk rotation</3>. Below is the combined shadow visibility map, which will be uniformly sampled in the subsequent GI pass.

Effects.title: Effects
Effects.content0: <1>The effects techniques used in the game</1>:
content1: <2>Call of Duty: Black Ops 6</2> contains a large number of visual effects: such as <3>SSFS</3> and <4>volumetric fog</4> generated mist effects, post-processing lighting effects (e.g. <5>Bloom</5> and <6>lens flares</6>), water rendering implemented based on the <7>Shallow Water Equations (SWE)</7>, hair rendering using a certain variant of the <8>Marschner model</8>, as well as <1>particle effects</1>, <1>HUD outline effects</1>, etc.

However, due to limited captured frames, even though the shader implementations of some effects have been identified by me, they do not appear in my limited footage. Therefore, I have selected some of the effects I analyzed in detail for demonstration (<9>download</9> the full document to view complete content).

SSFS.title: SSFS
SSFS.content1: <3>Screen-Space Fog Scattering (SSFS)</3> is a screen-space post-process that, in a first pass, normalizes scene depth, computes smooth depth-based weights and preliminary scattering contributions over small pixel neighborhoods, and in a second pass reads those intermediate results to apply brightness gain, accumulate, and normalize, delivering natural fog without costly 3D volume integration while remaining highly performant and easy to integrate.
SSFS.content2: The illustration above shows several key textures. In SSFS, multiple dispatches are used to perform successive fog-weight computations, ultimately producing the fog map shown below. In later rendering passes, this fog map is applied in a depth-dependent post-process fog effect (areas with greater depth receive stronger fog).

VolumetricFog.title: Volumetric Fog
VolumetricFog.content0: In the game, in addition to the post-process screen-space fog (SSFS), a ray-marching and froxel-based <3>volumetric fog</3> system is also used. <1>It is primarily divided into:</1>
VolumetricFog.content1: The volumetric fog rendering in this game uses a relatively common voxel-based approach: after computing the intersection between the fog volume’s <2>voxels</2> and the view-frustum <2>froxels</2> to generate the corresponding froxels, the fog effect is rendered via <1>ray marching</1>. The diagram below illustrates this principle:
VolumetricFog.content2: <1>Global volumetric fog is height-based fog.</1> In the image below, you can clearly see pronounced height fog in the sky—it’s obvious that the fog density correlates with world-space height, and I’ve even found direct evidence of this in the shader.
VolumetricFog.content3: <1>Local fog is primarily emitter fog.</1> In the image below, you can clearly see a distinct local volumetric fog effect, and there’s a corresponding implementation in the shader. The combination of <1>SSFS</1> and <1>volumetric fog</1> delivers exceptionally realistic fog effects in <2>Call of Duty: Black Ops 6</2>.

Bloom.title: Bloom
Bloom.content1: The <3>bloom effect</3> is also a common post-processing technique for better simulating real-world lighting. Notably, this game’s bloom implementation is <1>temporal</1>, effectively reducing flickering artifacts. The image above shows the <1>bloom-only</1> intermediate result; since its implementation is relatively straightforward, I won’t analyze it in depth here.

LensFlare.title: Lens Flare
LensFlare.content1: The <3>lens flare effect</3> is a common post-processing technique used to simulate the scattering and reflection of bright light sources within a camera lens. It typically works by identifying intensely bright areas in the scene (such as the sun or strong lights), then procedurally generating <1>ghost images</1> and streaks—often using chromatic aberration, anamorphic streak patterns, or circular halo kernels—and finally additively blending these artifacts over the rendered image to mimic real-world optical imperfections.

AE.title: Auto Exposure
content: Auto Exposure

Static.title: Static Geometry Rendering
Static.content0: <1>The static geometry rendering techniques used in the game</1>:
Static.content1: There are many optimization techniques for static geometry rendering to ensure that the mesh data in a single frame remains constrained and doesn’t overload the GPU—for example, Unreal Engine’s <1><3>Nanite</3></1>.

LOD.title: LOD
LOD.content1: As shown in the figure below, this draw call renders the leaves. You can see that leaf meshes farther from the camera use a lower LOD than those closer to the camera. This is a very common technique, so I won’t analyze it further (games typically have 4 LOD levels).

Culling.title: Culling
Culling.content1: Here, it’s evident that <1>cluster-based frustum culling</1> and <1>occlusion culling</1> are employed, which can reduce unnecessary mesh rendering and optimize performance.

Batching.title: Static Batching
Batching.content1: You can see that this single draw call contains almost all of the leaf static meshes, using a batching strategy to combine them—most likely <1>static batching</1> (though you can’t completely rule out some form of dynamic batching).
Batching.content2: Whether to use <1><2><3>Static Batching or GPU Instancing</3></2></1> is also a question worth discussing—I initially thought the game was using GPU Instancing, but it actually isn’t.

Abstract.title: Abstract
content: <1>Disclaimer</1>: This content is intended solely for educational and project showcase purposes. If any infringement is found, please <3>contact me</3> for prompt removal.

This blog presents a summary of my <1>rendering analysis</1> of <1><2><4>Infinity Nikki</4></2></1> and a review of the associated rendering techniques. To keep the blog concise, only key parts are highlighted here — for the full analysis, please download the detailed documentation. The full analysis document is available for download via the <1><5>Doc</5></1> button below the title.

PPLL.title: Per-Pixel Linked List OIT
PPLL.content1: <1><2><3>Per-Pixel Linked List (PPLL)</3></2></1> is a method for implementing Order-Independent Transparency (OIT). It constructs a linked list for each pixel to dynamically record all translucent fragments that pass through that pixel. Each fragment stores its color and depth information. During the rendering phase, all translucent fragments are inserted into the per-pixel lists. In the subsequent compositing phase, the fragments in each list are depth-sorted and blended one by one, resulting in a correct transparency effect regardless of the rendering order.
PPLL.content2: In <2>Infinity Nikki</2>, PPLL OIT is utilized, but unlike the typical implementation that uses a linked list structure to store per-pixel translucent values sorted by depth, this approach employs <1>two x4-sized buffers</1>, BufferA and BufferB as shown in the figure below, to store up to four color values and their corresponding depth information and indices per pixel. This means the system supports a maximum of four layers of translucent rendering.
PPLL.content3: Additionally, the <1><3>Shell-based fur</3></1> covered in the next section and <1>hair rendering</1> also involve transparency. BufferA and BufferB store not only the character's transparent clothing effects but also all alpha-blended data, which are composited together in a later dispatch.

ShellFur.title: Shell-Based Fur Rendering
ShellFur.content1: <1><2><3>Shell-based Fur Rendering</3></2></1> is a technique used to simulate the appearance of fur by layering multiple transparent shells along the surface normal of a 3D model. Each shell is slightly offset from the base surface and uses alpha-masked textures to represent scattered strands of fur. When rendered together with alpha blending, these layers create the illusion of volume and softness.
ShellFur.content2: We can see that the fur rendering in the game adopts a <1>4-layer Shell-Fur</1> technique. In the rendering shown above, shell layering is clearly visible at the edges—an artifact commonly associated with shell-based fur rendering. Nevertheless, the overall visual quality remains impressive. The four shell layers neatly fit into the ×4-sized PPLL buffers, enabling unified blending in subsequent passes.

SSAO.title: Screen Space Ambient Occlusion
SSAO.content1: <1><2><3>SSAO (Screen Space Ambient Occlusion)</3></2></1> is a widely used technique in real-time graphics to approximate ambient occlusion in screen space. Instead of evaluating geometry in world space, SSAO estimates the occlusion level of each pixel by analyzing the depth and normal information of neighboring pixels on the screen.
SSAO.content2: By decompiling the shader, we can see that the SSAO here does not directly use a normal buffer, but instead derives normals from the depth buffer. The auxiliary map may serve as a mask to enhance the AO effect (though this is not entirely certain). In this dispatch, an AO-only output is generated, as shown in the figure below, and will be used in subsequent rendering passes.

Abstract.title: Abstract
content: <1><2><3>RenderDoc</3></2></1> is currently one of the most effective tool for debugging the GPU. It is especially indispensable in the game industry for analyzing rendered frames.

However, <1>.rdc</1> files are not human-readable, which means we have to manually analyze them in RenderDoc each time. This makes the process inefficient and time-consuming. Therefore, there is a strong need for a convenient tool to address this issue — and that’s the motivation behind RDC-Parser.
You can download the detailed documentation by clicking the <1><4>Doc</4></1> button below the title.

Requirements.title: Requirements
content: RDC-Parser is required to parse the <1>RenderGraph</1> information from an .rdc file and export it into a JSON file, including associated Texture, Mesh, and Shader data. In addition, it should support command-line usage without launching RenderDoc.

In terms of functionality, future versions should also support visualizing the <1>.rdc</1> file as an interactive RenderGraph—similar to tools like <1><2><3>ARM Frame Advisor</3></2></1>—so that we can intuitively understand the full rendering pipeline. The following is the RenderGraph visualization from Frame Advisor.

Challenges.title: Challenges
content1: The main challenges arise when parsing large .rdc files. Taking a frame capture from Infinity Nikki as an example, there are two major performance bottlenecks:

list.0: The time complexity of RenderDoc's state-switching API is proportional to the size of the .rdc file.
list.1: Saving Textures, Meshes, and Shaders locally requires significant disk time, as each draw call contains a large amount of data—including Textures, Meshes, Shaders, and more—that needs to be parsed.

content2: I performed extensive optimizations, such as high-concurrency I/O tasks and texture deduplication (since many textures are not render targets and do not change between draw calls). As a result, using a frame capture from my Pika Engine as an example, I reduced the processing time from over 150 seconds to under 10 seconds.

Outcomes.title: Outcomes
content: The RDC-Parser tool constitutes only a portion of our group project and was the component I personally handled. Other modules not under my responsibility are beyond the scope of this description. Below is the test result of RDC-Parser parsing a captured frame from <1><2><3>Infinity Nikki</3></2></1>.

Abstract.title: Abstract
content: PUBGConfigUpgrader is a UE Commandlet plugin tool designed to automate the migration of configuration files for the <1><2><3>Game for Peace</3></2></1> (PUBG Mobile China) project from both the public UE4 and the Tencent’s internal Galaxy version of UE4 to UE5.4. It also includes customized modifications based on project team requirements to align with the features of UE5.4 and ensure compatibility with additional needs.
You can download the detailed documentation by clicking the <1><4>Doc</4></1> button below the title.

Requirements.title: Requirements
content: The project team required that UE5.4 maintain full compatibility with all UE4 functionalities, while also introducing many new configurations—such as support for some <1>HarmonyOS</1> devices (with several sensitive details omitted).

The tool reads data from three `.ini` configuration files of the public UE4 version and two from the Galaxy version, then generates three corresponding `.ini` files for UE5.4. It ensures that the user's original configurations—such as custom `CVars`—are preserved. Numerous additional special requirements have been omitted here.

Challenges.title: Challenges
content1: The original configuration files were highly complex, covering rendering settings for the Game for Peace lobby configurations, individual map configurations, device-specific settings, whitelists, and more.

My task was to extract all relevant information while generating the corresponding UE5.4 versions, discarding outdated entries for unsupported low-end devices, introducing finer-grained performance tiers for newer, higher-end models, and carrying out a series of related tasks. On top of that, I had to ensure that all general-purpose content from the original UE4 configurations could be correctly and appropriately migrated to UE5.4.

Outcomes.title: Outcomes
content: In the end, I successfully met all the requirements and delivered the PUBGConfigUpgrader automation tool.

Abstract.title: Abstract
content: ModelGray is a <1><2><3>ZBrush</3></2></1> and <1><2><4>Blender</4></2></1> plugin that I developed during my internship. It integrates directly into the software: when a user requests a model heightmap, the plugin sends the target image to the backend (Lightspeed Studios’ internal AI solution <1>LightAI</1>) and returns the result, greatly simplifying the workflow for artists creating relief models. The software is accessible only via the company intranet.
You can download the detailed documentation by clicking the <1><5>Doc</5></1> button below the title.

Requirements.title: Requirements
content: The project team aimed to <1>streamline the relief-model generation workflow</1> for artists. Unlike other relief plugins—which typically require jumping to a web page for AI generation (for example, the suite of plugins based on <1><2><3>OdysseyAI</3></2></1> solutions)—Lightspeed Studios’ internal AI solution, LightAI, also provides powerful model heightmap generation capabilities for relief creation. The team wanted to eliminate the intermediate web-based step and fetch results directly through the plugin, simplifying the sequence of target acquisition, network request, and result retrieval into a single seamless operation.

Challenges.title: Challenges
content1: The ZBrush version of the plugin faced several challenges, primarily due to the limitations of ZBrush's native scripting language, <1><3>ZScript</3></1>, which lacks many advanced capabilities.
content2: Due to these limitations, tasks such as HTTP/HTTPS requests and SSL encryption had to be handled by calling C++ code through ZScript.
The Blender version, on the other hand, was much more straightforward to develop, as it allowed direct implementation using <1>Python</1>.

Outcomes.title: Outcomes
content: ModelGray has been officially released for internal use by the company’s art team. Below are showcase images of the ZBrush and Blender plugin versions.
